For MoM: the mesh is on surfaces only. Converge on the edge length of the mesh triangles. Start at lambda/10, refine to lambda/15 and lambda/20 near edges, ports, and discontinuities where current density varies rapidly.

In all cases, refine the mesh more aggressively near geometric features: edges, corners, vias, narrow gaps, and slot apertures. These areas have rapidly varying fields or currents and dominate the simulation accuracy.

The convergence metric must be the quantity you care about. Converging on S11 at one frequency does not guarantee convergence of S21 at another frequency or the radiation pattern. Check convergence on all quantities of interest.
Record the final mesh statistics: number of elements, memory usage, solve time per frequency. This data is needed to estimate simulation time for future similar structures.

steps.description: Extract the simulation results (S-parameters, fields, patterns), compare to analytical predictions and measurements, and iterate if they disagree.

inputs.name: converged-mesh
inputs.desc: Converged simulation mesh and settings

inputs.name: em-model
inputs.desc: The EM model

inputs.name: analysis-goals
inputs.desc: Quantities to extract and accuracy targets

outputs.name: simulation-results
outputs.desc: Extracted S-parameters (Touchstone file), radiation patterns, field plots, and any derived quantities (impedance, gain, coupling)

outputs.name: simulation-measurement-correlation
outputs.desc: Comparison of simulation to measurement (if available) or analytical prediction, with analysis of discrepancies and model corrections

process: Extract S-parameters and export in Touchstone format for use in circuit simulators. Check passivity (|S11|^2 + |S21|^2 <= 1 for a lossless two-port) and reciprocity (S12 = S21 for passive structures). Violations indicate a simulation error.

For antennas: extract the far-field radiation pattern (gain in dBi vs. theta and phi), input impedance, efficiency (ratio of radiated power to accepted power), and bandwidth (frequency range where |S11| < -10 dB).

Visualize the current or field distribution at key frequencies. This provides physical insight: where is the current flowing, where are the losses, where is the radiation coming from. This understanding is more valuable than the numbers alone for diagnosing problems and making design improvements.

Compare to analytical predictions. For a microstrip line, the simulated impedance should agree with the analytical formula to within 1 to 2%. For a patch antenna, the resonant frequency should agree with the cavity model to within 2 to 3%. Larger discrepancies suggest a modeling error.

Compare to measurement when available. Common sources of discrepancy: dielectric constant different from nominal (measure it or use a trim coupon), conductor surface roughness (increases loss at high frequencies, model with Huray or Hammerstad correction), connector and probe transition effects (de-embed or include in the model).

If simulation and measurement disagree by more than the expected uncertainty, systematically vary model parameters (dielectric constant, loss tangent, conductor conductivity, dimensions) to identify which parameter, when corrected, brings the simulation into agreement. This calibrated model is then reliable for design variations.

description: Execute accurate RF measurements using vector network analyzers, spectrum analyzers, and power meters, with proper calibration and uncertainty analysis.

steps.description: Calibrate a vector network analyzer for accurate S-parameter measurement using the appropriate calibration method for the measurement scenario.

inputs.name: measurement-scenario
inputs.desc: What is being measured: coaxial DUT, on-wafer device, PCB fixture, waveguide component. Frequency range and port configuration.

inputs.name: calibration-standards
inputs.desc: Available calibration kit: SOLT (short-open-load-thru), TRL (thru-reflect-line), or electronic calibration module (ECal)

outputs.name: calibration-procedure
outputs.desc: Step-by-step calibration procedure for the measurement scenario, including the standards to apply and the order

outputs.name: calibration-verification
outputs.desc: Methods to verify calibration quality before proceeding with measurements

process: SOLT calibration (most common for coaxial measurements): connect Short, Open, Load (50 ohm), and Thru standards at the measurement plane. The VNA uses the known response of these standards to calculate 12 error terms (for a full 2-port calibration). Use the calibration kit matched to the connector type.

TRL calibration (for non-coaxial or high-accuracy measurements): requires a Thru (zero-length or known length), Reflect (short or open, same at both ports), and Line (transmission line of known impedance, length approximately lambda/4 at the center frequency). TRL is self-calibrating: the line impedance defines the reference impedance, and the reflect does not need to be characterized.

For on-wafer measurements (probing a chip or MMIC): use TRL or multiline TRL with on-wafer calibration standards fabricated on the same substrate. This de-embeds the probe-to-wafer transition. Verify by measuring a known on-wafer verification standard (through line of known length).

For fixture-based measurements (PCB test fixture): calibrate at the fixture connectors with SOLT, then de-embed the fixture using time-domain gating or a fixture characterization (measure the fixture itself and mathematically remove its effect).

Verify calibration quality: measure a known standard not used in the calibration (verification standard). For example, after SOLT calibration, measure a precision airline (known impedance and length). The measured S11 should be below -40 dB and S21 should match the airline's calculated loss. Also check that the Smith chart trace for an open is on the right side and for a short is on the left.
Note the calibration valid frequency range and the reference plane location. All subsequent measurements are only valid within this range and at this plane.

steps.description: Measure the S-parameters of a DUT with proper fixturing, including de-embedding of fixture effects and time-domain techniques for isolating reflections.

inputs.name: calibration-procedure
inputs.desc: Completed VNA calibration

inputs.name: dut-description
inputs.desc: Device under test: type, connectors, frequency range of interest

outputs.name: measured-s-parameters
outputs.desc: S-parameter data (S11, S21, S12, S22) across frequency in Touchstone format, with de-embedding applied if needed

outputs.name: measurement-uncertainty-estimate
outputs.desc: Estimated uncertainty in the measured S-parameters from connector repeatability, calibration residuals, and environmental factors

process: Connect the DUT to the calibrated VNA ports. Use consistent torque on connectors (8 in-lb for SMA, 12 in-lb for N-type) with a torque wrench. Inconsistent connector torque is the single largest source of measurement error in coaxial measurements.

Set the VNA parameters: start and stop frequency (matching calibration range), number of points (enough to resolve features; 401 or 801 typical), IF bandwidth (narrower = lower noise floor but slower; 1 kHz for general, 10 Hz for high dynamic range), and power level (in the linear range of the DUT, typically -10 to 0 dBm for passive devices).

Measure and inspect all four S-parameters. For a passive reciprocal device, S12 should equal S21. If they differ by more than the measurement uncertainty, check for a bad connection or calibration drift.

Use time-domain gating to isolate the DUT response from fixture effects when de-embedding is not practical. Transform the frequency-domain S-parameters to time domain (inverse FFT). Gate (window) around the DUT response, excluding reflections from connectors and fixture transitions. Transform back to frequency domain.
For differential (balanced) devices: measure all four single-ended S-parameters of the 4-port, then convert to mixed-mode S-parameters (Sdd, Scc, Sdc, Scd) using the mixed-mode transformation matrix.

Estimate measurement uncertainty: connector repeatability (measure, disconnect, reconnect, measure again; the variation is the repeatability uncertainty, typically 0.01 to 0.05 in |S11|). Add calibration residual error, cable stability (flexing cables changes S-parameters), and temperature variation during the measurement.

steps.description: Measure RF signal power, spectral content, and spurious emissions using spectrum analyzers and power meters with appropriate detector and bandwidth settings.

inputs.name: signal-description
inputs.desc: Signal to measure: CW, pulsed, modulated, or noise-like. Approximate frequency and power level.

inputs.name: measurement-requirement
inputs.desc: What needs to be measured: absolute power, spectral shape, spurious emissions, phase noise, or occupied bandwidth

outputs.name: spectrum-measurement-result
outputs.desc: Measured spectrum or power with the instrument settings used and any corrections applied

outputs.name: measurement-accuracy-assessment
outputs.desc: Assessment of measurement accuracy including instrument uncertainty, mismatch loss, and any corrections

process: For absolute power measurement: a calibrated power meter (thermal or diode sensor) is more accurate than a spectrum analyzer. Thermal sensors measure true RMS power regardless of waveform (accurate for any signal type, limited dynamic range). Diode sensors are more sensitive but only accurate for CW unless they have a wide dynamic range mode.

Spectrum analyzer RBW selection: RBW determines the noise floor and frequency resolution. For CW signals, RBW does not affect the displayed amplitude (the signal is narrower than any RBW). For noise-like signals, displayed power changes with RBW: P_displayed = P_noise_density + 10*log10(RBW). For modulated signals, set RBW wider than the signal bandwidth to capture total power, or use channel power measurement mode.
Spectrum analyzer VBW: video bandwidth smooths the display. For noise measurements, set VBW <= RBW/3 to reduce measurement variance. For CW, VBW can equal RBW for faster sweep.

Detector type: peak detector shows the highest instantaneous value in each display bin (standard for spurious searches). Sample detector samples one point per bin (correct for noise power measurements). Average detector averages all samples in each bin (reduces variance). RMS detector computes true RMS of each bin (best for accurate power measurement of any signal type).

For spurious emission measurement: scan a wide frequency range with the RBW set narrow enough to resolve the spurious from the noise floor but wide enough for reasonable sweep time. First do a wide scan to locate spurs, then zoom in on each spur with narrower RBW for accurate level measurement.

Apply corrections: cable loss between DUT and instrument (add it back to the measured power), mismatch loss (from VSWR of source and load), and any attenuator at the instrument input. For precise measurements, measure the cable loss on the VNA and apply it frequency by frequency.

steps.description: Measure phase noise of oscillators and radiation patterns of antennas using specialized techniques and setups.

inputs.name: measurement-requirement
inputs.desc: Phase noise measurement of an oscillator/synthesizer, or antenna pattern measurement

inputs.name: dut-description
inputs.desc: Device under test with approximate specifications

outputs.name: specialized-measurement-result
outputs.desc: Phase noise plot (dBc/Hz vs. offset) or antenna pattern (gain vs. angle in E-plane and H-plane) with measurement setup documented

outputs.name: measurement-limitations
outputs.desc: Known limitations of the measurement: instrument noise floor, dynamic range, angular resolution, and any corrections or assumptions

process: Phase noise measurement via direct spectrum: tune the spectrum analyzer to the carrier, set RBW to the offset of interest (e.g., 1 kHz RBW for 10 kHz offset measurement), and measure the noise power in that bandwidth. L(f) = P_noise_in_1Hz_BW - P_carrier = P_measured - P_carrier - 10*log10(RBW) + correction_factors. This method is limited by the spectrum analyzer's own phase noise.

Phase noise measurement via PLL-based method (signal source analyzer): the instrument locks an internal clean reference to the DUT, and the PLL error voltage represents the phase noise. This method has a lower noise floor than direct spectrum, especially at close-in offsets. Cross-correlation (two independent measurement channels averaged) reduces the floor further, by 5*log10(N_correlations) dB.

For antenna pattern measurement: set up the DUT on a positioner in an anechoic chamber or on an outdoor range. The source antenna illuminates the DUT from the far field (minimum distance 2*D^2/lambda). Rotate the DUT in azimuth and elevation while recording the received power.

For near-field to far-field: scan the near field on a planar surface (for directive antennas) or spherical surface (for omnidirectional). Sample spacing must be less than lambda/2 (Nyquist). The far field is computed by Fourier transform of the measured near-field data. This method is more compact and controlled than a far-field range.

Measure gain by substitution: in the same setup, replace the DUT with a standard gain horn of known gain. The DUT gain = horn_gain + (P_received_DUT - P_received_horn). This eliminates path loss and cable loss from the calculation.

Document the measurement limitations: anechoic chamber quiet zone size and reflectivity level, positioner alignment accuracy, source antenna pattern (any illumination taper across the DUT aperture reduces measured gain), and cable flexing during rotation (use a rotary joint or route cables to minimize movement).
